belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

Let’s start with the business case. 

The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It is what earns the project its support. People outside the team only back what they can understand and size — and it is the first thing the Define report shows.

Here’s a worked example to illustrate what a good business case looks like:

"During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month." (This is an illustration — not your data.)

Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves time and resources, outlining what is wrong, where, since when, how big it is, and the cost.

reply.answer:
Welcome to Measure. Quick recap of what Define locked in, so we're building on the same picture:

• **Problem:** From January to June 2026, 23% of supplier invoices were paid after their 30-day terms, affecting suppliers and ward managers. Late payments result in interest charges, lost discounts, and supplier stops, with delays occurring during the resolve mismatches and approve steps. Suppliers chase payments via phone and email, and some put us on stop.
• **Baseline:** Late payment rate: 23%, January–June 2026, from the AP ledger.
• **Target:** Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices by 31 March 2027.
• **Process (SIPOC):** Invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites, measuring days from invoice receipt to payment release, and the share of invoices with a match exception.

Now, what Measure actually does: we expand that SIPOC into a detailed process map, decide what to collect and how, check the measurement itself can be trusted, confirm the process is behaving consistently, establish a real baseline, and prioritise which inputs are most likely driving the problem. You don't need to hold these in a fixed order in your head — I'll guide you — but here's the full menu so nothing's a surprise:

**Required (7)**
□ Detailed process map — timings, people, value vs waste per step
□ Data collection plan — what, how much, how often, who
□ Stability check — is the process behaving consistently?
□ Baseline — the current level, once we trust the data
□ Cause prioritisation — scoring what might be driving it
□ Vital few X's — the shortlist Analyse will test
□ Issues and barriers — what's in your way

**Recommended (3)**
□ Sigma level · □ Measurement system check · □ Secondary metrics

**Progress: 0 of 7 required complete**

We'll work through these roughly in the order above, and I'll flag the two recommended ones — the measurement system check and the sigma level — when we reach them, rather than saving them for the end. First up: expanding your Define map, because everything else attaches to it. Let me show you what that looks like.

define_structured.voc_summary: Our customers are the suppliers, who need paying on the agreed 30-day terms, and our own ward managers, who need stock to keep arriving. Suppliers complain most about payments arriving late and not knowing when they will be paid; ward managers about deliveries being held. One more thing: suppliers also told us they cannot see the status of an invoice once it is submitted.
define_structured.problem_statement: From January to June 2026, 23% of supplier invoices were paid after their 30-day terms, affecting suppliers and ward managers. Late payments result in interest charges, lost discounts, and supplier stops, with delays occurring during the resolve mismatches and approve steps. Suppliers chase payments via phone and email, and some put us on stop.

baseline_estimate.raw: One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.

project_scope.in_scope: Invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites.
project_scope.out_scope: Non-PO invoices, payroll, procurement tendering, and the ERP system itself.

define_structured.goal_statement: Reduce the late payment rate from 23% to under 5% by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.

target_value.raw: Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices.

define_structured.target_date: We plan to finish the project by 31 March 2027 (2027-03-31).

benefits_analysis.cost_of_gap: About £68,000 a year in interest and lost discounts, from the savings calculation.
benefits_analysis.realisation_schedule: It would start in Q2 2027 at about £17,000 a quarter.
benefits_analysis.finance_contact: Sam Reid, management accountant, who will validate it.

define_structured.secondary_metrics: Two things must not get worse: the number of supplier payment queries the AP team handles each month, and AP staff overtime hours. Both should stay at or below today's levels.

problems.note: approvers on leave and nobody covers

share of invoices with a match exception

define_structured.issues_and_barriers: Two barriers: the three sites use different approval routes, and an ERP change freeze until January limits system changes. One risk: AP staff turnover over the winter.

critical_to_quality.need: Need stock to keep arriving; complain most about deliveries being held.
critical_to_quality.requirement: No supplier puts us on stop in a quarter.

result.calculation_note: (23% baseline − 5% target) × 42000 units/year × 9 per unit = 68040 a year. Check the units agree: the rates are shares of the yearly volume, and the unit cost is the cost of one defect.
